nodes.statement: \emph{Case 3.1:} If $d_2 > x^{1/5 - 5\delta}$ and $d_3 \le x^{1/3+2\delta}/N$, we set $D_1 := Nx^{-\delta}$, $D_2 := d_2$, and $D_3 := x^{3/5 - 3\delta}/(Nd_2)$, which have $D_i \ge d_i$ (in light of \cref{eq:fact-satisfying}) and $D_1 D_2 D_3 \ge D$. We then run a greedy process to place the remaining primes $p_k$ with $k \ge j+1$ into either $d_1$ or $d_3$, while preserving the inequalities $d_i \le D_i$. This works because at step $k$, before placing $p_k$, we have \[ p_1 \cdots p_{k-1} p_k^2 \le D \qquad\quad \Rightarrow \qquad\quad p_k^2 \le \frac{D}{d_1 d_2 d_3} \le \frac{D_1 D_3}{d_1 d_3}, \] so $p_k \le \max(D_1/d_1, D_3/d_3)$ (i.e., there is ``enough room'' for $p_k$ in $d_1$ or $d_3$). In the end, we have $d = d_1 d_2 d_3$ with $d_i \le D_i$, and we can verify the bounds in \cref{eq:system-to-verify} using $x^{1/5 - 5\delta} < d_2 \le x^{4/15-5\delta}$: \[ N^2 d_2 d_3^2 \le N^2 d_2 \left(\frac{x^{3/5-3\delta}}{Nd_2}\right)^2 = \frac{x^{6/5 - 6\delta}}{d_2} < x^{1-\delta}, \] \[ N^2 d_2^5 d_3^2 \le N^2 d_2^5 \left(\frac{x^{3/5-3\delta}}{Nd_2}\right)^2 = d_2^3 x^{6/5-6\delta} \le x^{2-\delta}. \]
nodes.name: Case 3.1
nodes.statement_short: If $d_2$ is large, set $D_3=x^{3/5-3\delta}/(Nd_2)$ and fill $d_1,d_3$ greedily.

nodes.statement: \emph{Case 3.2:} Otherwise, we have $d_2 \le x^{1/5-5\delta}$ and $d_3 > x^{1/3+2\delta}/N$. We then set $D_1 := N x^{-\delta}$, $D_2 := x^{3/5-3\delta}/(Nd_3)$, and $D_3 := d_3$, which have $D_i \ge d_i$ (in light of \cref{eq:fact-satisfying}) and $D_1 D_2 D_3 \ge D$. We run a similar greedy process to place the remaining primes $p_k$ with $k \ge j+1$ into either $d_1$ or $d_2$, while preserving the bounds $d_i \le D_i$. This works because at step $k$, before placing $p_k$, we have \[ p_1 \cdots p_{k-1} p_k^2 \le D \qquad\quad \Rightarrow \qquad\quad p_k^2 \le \frac{D}{d_1 d_2 d_3} \le \frac{D_1 D_2}{d_1 d_2}, \] so $p_k \le \max(\frac{D_1}{d_1}, \frac{D_2}{d_2})$. In the end, we have $d = d_1 d_2 d_3$ with $d_i \le D_i$, and we can verify the bounds in \cref{eq:system-to-verify} using $x^{1/3 + 2\delta}/N < d_3 \le x^{2/5 + 2\delta}/N$: \[ N^2 d_2 d_3^2 \le N^2 \frac{x^{3/5-3\delta}}{Nd_3} d_3^2 = N d_3\, x^{3/5 - 3\delta} \le x^{1-\delta}, \] \[ N^2 d_2^5 d_3^2 \le N^2 \left(\frac{x^{3/5-3\delta}}{Nd_3}\right)^5 d_3^2 = \frac{x^{3-15\delta}}{(Nd_3)^3} \le x^{2-\delta}. \] We have now covered all cases.
nodes.name: Case 3.2
nodes.statement_short: If $d_3$ is large, set $D_2=x^{3/5-3\delta}/(Nd_3)$ and fill $d_1,d_2$ greedily.

nodes.statement: Let $(D_1, D_2) := (N x^{-\delta}, x^{\vartheta-\delta}/N)$, so that $D \le D_1 D_2$ and $D_i \ge 1$. Let $d_1 = d_2 = 1$ and $d = p_1\cdots p_r$, where $p_1 \ge \cdots \ge p_r$ are primes. We will run a greedy algorithm to append each of these primes to one of $d_1$ or $d_2$, while preserving the bounds $d_1 \le D_1$, $d_2 \le D_2$. At step $j \ge 1$, the definition of $\mathcal{D}^{\textnormal{well}}(D)$ implies \[ p_j^2 = \frac{p_1\cdots p_{j-1} p_j^2}{p_1\cdots p_{j-1}} \le \frac{D}{p_1 \cdots p_{j-1}} \le \frac{D_1 D_2}{d_1 d_2}, \] so $p_j \le \max(D_1/d_1, D_2/d_2)$, and we can append $p_j$ to one of $d_1$ and $d_2$. In the end, we take $d_3 = 1$, and obtain $d = d_1d_2d_3$ with $d_1 \le D_1$, $d_2 \le D_2$. To verify the system \cref{eq:system-to-verify}, we write \[ d_1 \le D_1 = \frac{N}{x^\delta}, \] \[ N^2 d_2 d_3^2 \le N^2 D_2 = N x^{\vartheta-\delta} \le x^{1/3+\delta+2/3-2\delta} = x^{1-\delta}, \] and, using the hypothesis in the form $D_2 = x^{\vartheta-\delta}/N \le x^{(2-2\vartheta)/3}$, \[ N^2 d_2^5 d_3^2 \le (ND_2)^2 D_2^3 \le x^{2(\vartheta-\delta)} x^{2-2\vartheta} \le x^{2-\delta}, \] as required.

nodes.statement: Let $(D_1, D_2, D_3) := (Nx^{-\delta}, x^v, x^{1-\vartheta-\delta}/N)$, so that $D \le D_1 D_2 D_3$ and $D_i \ge 1$. Note that any tuple $(d_1, d_2, d_3)$ with $d_i \le D_i$ satisfies \cref{eq:system-to-verify}, since \[ N^2 D_2 D_3^2 = x^{v + 2-2\vartheta-2\delta} = x^{1-2\delta}, \] and using $\vartheta \le \tfrac{5}{8}$, \[ N^2 D_2^5 D_3^2 = x^{5v + 2-2\vartheta-2\delta} = x^{8\vartheta-3-2\delta} \le x^{2-2\delta}. \] By assumption, we have ($p_1 \le D_2$ and $p_2^2 \le D_1D_3$) or ($p_2 \le D_2$ and $p_1^2 \le D_1D_3$), so for some choice $\{d_1, d_2, d_3\} = \{1, p_1, p_2\}$ we must have $d_i \le D_i$ for all $i$. We keep this choice, and run a greedy algorithm to append the primes $p_j$, for $j \ge 3$, to one of $d_1, d_2, d_3$ (i.e., $d_i \gets d_ip_j$), while preserving the bounds $d_i \le D_i$. If this algorithm terminates after appending all primes $p_3, \ldots, p_r$, then we obtain a factorization $d = d_1d_2d_3$ which satisfies $d_i \le D_i$, and thus also \cref{eq:system-to-verify}. Otherwise, there must be some index $3 \le j \le r$ such that the prime $p_j$ cannot be appended to any $d_i$, where $d_1d_2d_3 = p_1\cdots p_{j-1}$; thus we have $d_ip_j > D_i$ for all $i$. By our assumption, we thus have \[ x^v = D_2 < d_2p_j \le D_2p_3 \le x^v x^{u-v} = x^u, \] so $d_2' := d_2p_j \in [x^v, x^u]$, and \[ D_1 < d_1 p_j = \frac{d_1d_2d_3p_j^2}{d_2d_3p_j} \le \frac{D}{d_2d_3p_j} \le \frac{D_1 D_2 D_3}{d_2'd_3}, \] so $D_3' := D_2 D_3/d_2' \ge d_3$. By the definition of $\mathcal{D}^{\textnormal{well}}(D)$ we have that for each $k > j$, \[ p_k^2 \le \frac{D}{p_1\cdots p_{k-1}} \le \frac{D_1D_2D_3}{d_1d_2d_3 p_j \cdots p_{k-1}} = \frac{D_1D_3'}{d_1d_3p_{j+1} \cdots p_{k-1}}. \] Using this bound, we can greedily construct a factorization $d_1' d_3' = d_1d_3 p_{j+1} \cdots p_r$ (starting from $d_1' = d_1$, $d_3' = d_3$ and appending each $p_k$ at a time) such that $d_1' \le D_1$ and $d_3' \le D_3'$. Therefore, we have $d_1'd_2'd_3' = d$ and \[ d_1' \le D_1 = \frac{N}{x^{\delta}}, \qquad d_2' = d_2p_j \in [x^v, x^u], \qquad d_2'd_3' \le d_2'D_3' = D_2D_3 = \frac{x^{\vartheta-\delta}}{N}. \] By \cref{lem:general-factorization}, we conclude that $d_1', d_2', d_3'$ satisfy \cref{eq:system-to-verify}.

nodes.statement: Assuming $(iv)$, the conclusion follows immediately from \cref{lem:greedy-algorithm}. So let us assume that one of $(i)$, $(ii)$, $(iii)$ holds. Let $D_1 := N x^{-\delta}$, $d_2$ be the corresponding value from $(i)$, $(ii)$, or $(iii)$ (say, the first of these that holds), and \[ D_3 := \max\left(1, \frac{x^{\vartheta-\delta}}{Nd_2}\right). \] Note that $D \le D_1d_2D_3$ and $D_1, D_3 \ge 1$. If we can find a factorization $d = d_1d_2d_3$ with $d_1 \le D_1$ and $d_3 \le D_3$, then \cref{lem:general-factorization} will complete the proof. Suppose for a start that $d_2 = p_1 \cdots p_i \in [x^v, x^u]$ for some $i \in \{1, 2, 3\}$ as in $(i)$. For each $j \in \{i+1, \cdots, r\}$, by the definition of $\mathcal{D}^{\textnormal{well}}$ we have \[ p_j^2 \le \frac{D}{p_1 \cdots p_{j-1}} \le \frac{D_1 D_3}{p_{i+1}\cdots p_{j-1}}. \] Using this bound, we can greedily construct a factorization $d_1 d_3 = p_{i+1} \cdots p_r$ (starting from $d_1 = 1$, $d_3 = 1$ and appending each $p_j$ at a time) such that $d_1 \le D_1$ and $d_3 \le D_3$, so we are done. Otherwise, we have $p_1, p_1p_2, p_1p_2p_3 \not\in [x^v, x^u]$; in particular, $p_1 \le x^u$ and $p_1 \not \in [x^v, x^u]$ imply $p_1 < x^v$, so $p_2 < x^v$ as well; thus $(i)$ cannot hold. \begin{itemize} \item If $(ii)$ holds, so $d_2 := p_1p_3 \in [x^v, x^u]$ and $p_2^2 \le x^{\vartheta-2\delta}/d_2 \le D_1 D_3$, then we have $p_2 \le D_1$ or $p_2 \le D_3$. \item If $(iii)$ holds, so $d_2 := p_2p_3 \in [x^v, x^u]$ and $p_1^2 \le x^{\vartheta-2\delta}/d_2 \le D_1 D_3$, then we have $p_1 \le D_1$ or $p_1 \le D_3$. \end{itemize} In either case, we can factor $p_1p_2p_3 = d_1d_2d_3$ where $d_1 \le D_1$ and $d_3 \le D_3$. Then for each $j \in \{4, \ldots, r\}$ (if any), we have \[ p_j^2 \le \frac{D}{p_1 \cdots p_{j-1}} \le \frac{D_1d_2D_3}{p_1 \cdots p_{j-1}} \le \frac{(D_1/d_1) (D_3/d_3)}{p_4 \cdots p_{j-1}}, \] so we can greedily append $p_j$ to one of $d_1$ and $d_3$ until we have $d = d_1d_2d_3$ with $d_1 \le D_1$, $d_3 \le D_3$.

nodes.statement: Let $d = p_1\cdots p_r$ where $p_1 \ge \cdots \ge p_r$ are primes with $p_i = x^{t_i}$. Consider the set $I$ of all exponents $\vartheta_0 \in [0, 1)$ such that if $d \in \mathcal{D}^{\textnormal{well}}(x^{\vartheta_0})$, then there exists a factorization $d = d_1 d_2 d_3$ into positive integers obeying \cref{eq:system-to-verify}. Since $\mathcal{D}^{\textnormal{well}}(D) \subset \mathcal{D}^{\textnormal{well}}(D')$ when $D \le D'$, $I$ is an interval of the form $[0, \vartheta_{\max})$; our goal is to show that $\vartheta(t_1) - 2\delta \in I$ as in \cref{eq:vartheta-t}, and moreover, if $t_1 \le \tfrac{1}{4}$ and $r \ge 3$, then $\vartheta(t_1, t_2, t_3) - 4\delta \in I$ as in \cref{eq:vartheta-123}. Applying \cref{prop:fact-anatomy} for some $\vartheta \in [\tfrac{1}{2}, \tfrac{5}{8}]$, we deduce that $\vartheta - 2\delta \in I$ provided $t_1 \le u$, and that one of the following holds: \begin{itemize} \item[$(i)$.] $t \in [v, u]$ for some $t \in \{t_1, t_2, t_1 + t_2, t_1 + t_2 + t_3\}$; \item[$(ii)$.] $t_1 + t_3 \in [v, u]$ and $t_1 + 2t_2 + t_3 \le \vartheta - 2\delta$; \item[$(iii)$.] $t_2 + t_3 \in [v, u]$ and $2t_1 + t_2 + t_3 \le \vartheta - 2\delta$; \item[$(iv)$.] $t_3 \le u - v$ and $t_1 \le v$, $2t_2 \le 1 - \vartheta - 2\delta$; \item[$(v)$.] $t_3 \le u - v$ and $t_2 \le v$, $2t_1 \le 1 - \vartheta - 2\delta$. \end{itemize} Recalling the definitions of $\vartheta(t)$ and $u, v$ from \cref{eq:u-v-choice,eq:vartheta-t}, a short computation gives \[ t \in [u, v] = \left[2\vartheta - 1, \frac{2-2\vartheta}{3} \right] \qquad \iff \qquad \vartheta \le \vartheta(t) = \min\left(\frac{1+t}{2}, \frac{2-3t}{2}\right). \] Using $t = t_1$ in $(i)$, which automatically satisfies $t_1 \le u$, we deduce that \[ \vartheta(t_1) - 2\delta \in I, \] as required. Now assume that $t_1 \le \tfrac{1}{4}$ and $r \ge 3$; then we have $t_1 \le \tfrac{1}{4} \le (2-2\vartheta)/3 = u$ for any $\vartheta \le \tfrac{5}{8}$, so the condition $t_1 \le u$ holds automatically. Thus points $(i)$-$(v)$ above imply, respectively: \begin{itemize} \item[$(i)$.] $\max\{\vartheta(t_1), \vartheta(t_2), \vartheta(t_1+t_2), \vartheta(t_1+t_2+t_3)\} - 2\delta \in I$; \item[$(ii)$.] $\vartheta(t_1+t_3) - 2\delta \in I$ if the range $[t_1 + 2t_2 + t_3 + 2\delta, \vartheta(t_1+t_3)]$ is nonempty; \item[$(iii)$.] $\vartheta(t_2 + t_3) - 2\delta \in I$ if the range $[2t_1 + t_2 + t_3 + 2\delta, \vartheta(t_2+t_3)]$ is nonempty; \item[$(iv)$.] $\min\left\{ \tfrac{5-3t_3}{8}, 1-2t_2-2\delta\right \} - 2\delta \in I$ if $[\tfrac{1+t_1}{2}, \min\left\{ \tfrac{5-3t_3}{8}, 1-2t_2-2\delta\right \} - 2\delta]$ is nonempty; \item[$(v)$.] $\min\left\{ \tfrac{5-3t_3}{8}, 1-2t_1-2\delta\right \} - 2\delta \in I$ if $[\tfrac{1+t_2}{2}, \min\left\{ \tfrac{5-3t_3}{8}, 1-2t_1-2\delta\right \} - 2\delta]$ is nonempty. \end{itemize} Putting these together, using the cutoff function $\psi(x, y) = x \mathbbm{1}_{x \ge y+4\delta}$ to encode the nonemptiness of the required ranges above, and recalling \cref{eq:vartheta-123}, we conclude that \[ \vartheta(t_1, t_2, t_3) - 4\delta \in I, \] as required.

eq 0}} \phi(h, h') \sum_{\substack{k, \ell \ (k, dn_0nn'\ell) = 1}} \Phi\left( rac{\ell}{L},  rac{k}{K}ight) e\left( rac{e\overline{dn_0nn'\ell}}{k}ight) ight \vert. \] We then put $n_0$, $e \gets |e|$, and $q = dn_0 n n'$ in dyadic ranges, and use the divisor bound to write  egin{equation} \mathcal{K}(n 
eq n') \ll x^{o(1)} \sup_{\substack{N_0 \ll N \ E \ll |a| THN/N_0 \ Q \asymp d N^2/N_0}} \mathcal{K}_2(N_0, E, Q), \end{equation} where \[  egin{aligned} \mathcal{K}_2 &:= \sum_{q \sim Q} \max_{\substack{n_0 \le 2N \ n, n' \sim N/n_0 \ (n, n') = 1 \ 1 \le |t| \le T}} \left \vert \sum_{e \sim E} \sum_{\substack{h, h' \ at(n'h - nh') = \pm e}} \phi(h, h') \sum_{\substack{k, \ell \ (k, q\ell) = 1}} \Phi_0\left( rac{\ell}{L}ight) \Phi_0\left( rac{k}{K}ight) e\left( rac{\pm e \overline{q\ell}}{k}ight) ight \vert \ &= \sum_{q \sim Q} \left \vert \sum_{e \sim E} a_{e,q} \sum_{\substack{k, \ell \ (k, q\ell) = 1}} \Phi_0\left( rac{\ell}{L}ight) \Phi_0\left( rac{k}{K}ight) e\left( rac{\pm e \overline{q\ell}}{k}ight) ight \vert. \end{aligned} \] Above, we denoted \[ a_{e,q} := \sum_{\substack{h, h' \in \mathbb{Z} \ \pm at(q)(n'(q)h - n(q)h') = e}} \phi(h, h') \] if the maximum on the first line is attained at some $n(q), n'(q), t(q)$; if the maximum is empty, we let $a_{e,q} = 0$. Then by \cref{prop:large-sieve-additive}, we know that $(q, E, x, (a_{e,q})_{e \sim E}, A_q, Y)$ satisfies \cref{ass:large-sieve}, where \[ Y :=  rac{E H}{|a|(H+N/N_0)(N/N_0) \min_i T_H(\alpha_i)}, \quad A_q := \left(\sum_{e \sim E} |a_{e,q}|^2ight)^{1/2} + \sqrt{TE} \sqrt{ rac{H N_0}{N} +  rac{H^2 N_0^2}{N^2}}. \] Since $\min_i T_H(\alpha_i) \ll x^{2\varepsilon}$, we further have \[ Y \gg_\varepsilon x^{-2\varepsilon} rac{E H N_0}{|a|(H+N)N}. \] From \cref{prop:kloosterman-incomplete}, we conclude that \[ \mathcal{K}_2 \ll_{\varepsilon,a} x^{2\varepsilon} \|A_q\|_2 \left(L^2 E Q + \left(1 +  rac{K^2}{Q^2  rac{EHN_0}{(H+N)N}}ight)^{	heta_{\max}} K (K + LQ)(Q + E) ight)^{1/2}. \] Now by the same computation as in \cref{eq:primes-l2-bound} (incorporating a sum over $1 \le |t| \le T$, $t \mid e$), we have \[ \|A_q\|_2^2 \ll_\varepsilon x^{2\varepsilon} T E(HN + H^2 N_0), \] so that (using $|a| \le x^{\varepsilon}$) \[ \mathcal{K}_2 \ll_{\varepsilon} x^{4\varepsilon} \sqrt{T E(HN + H^2 N_0)} \left(L^2 E Q + \left(1 +  rac{K^2 (H+N)N}{Q^2 EHN_0}ight)^{	heta_{\max}} K (K + LQ)(Q + E) ight)^{1/2}. \] Since this right-hand side is non-decreasing in $E$ (due to $	heta_{\max} \le 1$), we may use the bounds $E \ll |a|THN/N_0$, $Q \asymp dN^2/N_0$ from \cref{eq:K-off-diag-split}, and $d \le x^{2\varepsilon}$ to obtain \[  egin{aligned} &\mathcal{K}_2 \ll_{\varepsilon} x^{5\varepsilon} \sqrt{T  rac{THN}{N_0}(HN + H^2 N_0)} \ &	imes \left(L^2  rac{THN}{N_0}  rac{N^2}{N_0} + \left(1 +  rac{K^2 (H+N)N}{\left( rac{N^2}{N_0}ight)^2  rac{THN}{N_0} HN_0}ight)^{	heta_{\max}} K \left(K + L rac{N^2}{N_0}ight)\left( rac{N^2}{N_0} +  rac{THN}{N_0}ight) ight)^{1/2}. \end{aligned} \] Since $	heta_{\max} \le 1/2$, this bound is seen to be non-increasing in the $N_0 \gg 1$ parameter; plugging this into \cref{eq:K-off-diag-split} and using the assumption $TH \ll N$, we conclude that \[  egin{aligned} \mathcal{K}(n 
eq n') \ll_{\varepsilon} x^{6\varepsilon} THN \left(L^2 TH N^3 + \left(1 +  rac{K^2}{N^3 TH^2}ight)^{	heta_{\max}} K \left(K + LN^2ight)N^2 ight)^{1/2}, \end{aligned} \] which gives the right-hand side of \cref{eq:consequence-incomplete}.
nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 6.1
nodes.statement_short: Split into diagonal $n=n'$ and off-diagonal terms, apply the general and additive large sieves with Proposition 3.7, and optimize dyadic parameters.

nodes.statement: Let $\mathcal{K}$ denote the sum in question; we begin by splitting \begin{equation} \mathcal{K} = \mathcal{K}(n = n') + \mathcal{K}(n \neq n'), \end{equation} where after a rescaling of the $e$ variable, \[ \mathcal{K}(n = n') := \sum_{n \sim N} \left \vert \sum_{\substack{1 \le |t| \le T \\ (t, n) = 1}} \sum_{\substack{h, h' \\ e = at(h - h') \neq 0}} \phi(h, h') \sum_{\substack{k, \ell \\ (k, dn\ell) = 1}} \Phi\left(\frac{\ell}{L}, \frac{k}{K}\right) e\left(\frac{e\overline{dn\ell}}{k}\right) \right \vert. \]
nodes.name: Split diagonal/off-diagonal
nodes.statement_short: Split $\mathcal K$ into $n=n'$ and $n\neq n'$.

nodes.statement: \mathcal{K} = \mathcal{K}(n = n') + \mathcal{K}(n \neq n'),
nodes.name: Equation (6.2) eq:K-split-smooth
nodes.label: eq:K-split-smooth

nodes.statement: The dominant contribution will come from $\mathcal{K}(n \neq n')$, but let us first bound the simpler sum $\mathcal{K}(n = n')$. Setting $e \gets |e|$, putting $e$ and $q = dn$ in dyadic ranges and denoting \[ a_{e,q} := \mathbbm{1}_{d \mid q} \sum_{\substack{1 \le |t| \le T \\ (t, q/d) = 1 \\ h,h' \in \mathbb{Z} \\ \pm at(h-h') = e}} \phi(h,h'), \] we get \begin{equation} \mathcal{K}(n = n') \ll x^{o(1)} \sup_{\substack{E \ll |a|TH \\ Q \asymp dN}} \mathcal{K}_1(E, Q), \end{equation} where \[ \mathcal{K}_1 = \sum_{q \sim Q} \left \vert \sum_{e \sim E} a_{e,q} \sum_{\substack{k, \ell \\ (k, q\ell) = 1}} \Phi\left(\frac{\ell}{L}, \frac{k}{K}\right) e\left(\frac{\pm e\overline{q\ell}}{k}\right) \right \vert. \]
nodes.name: Diagonal setup
nodes.statement_short: For $n=n'$, put $e$ and $q=dn$ in dyadic ranges and define $a_{e,q}$.

nodes.statement: \mathcal{K}(n = n') \ll x^{o(1)} \sup_{\substack{E \ll |a|TH \\ Q \asymp dN}} \mathcal{K}_1(E, Q),
nodes.name: Equation (6.3) eq:K-diag-split
nodes.label: eq:K-diag-split

nodes.statement: We recall that by \cref{prop:large-sieve-general}, the tuple $(q, E, 1, (a_{e,q})_{e \sim E}, \|(a_{e,q})_{e \sim E}\|_2, 1)$ satisfies \cref{ass:large-sieve}. So by \cref{prop:kloosterman-incomplete} with $S = 1$ (which uses none of our new large sieve technology in this instance), we have \[ \mathcal{K}_1 \ll x^{o(1)} \|(a_{e,q})_{e \sim E, q \sim Q} \|_2 \left(L^2 E Q + \left(1 + \frac{K^2}{Q^2}\right)^{\theta_{\max}} K (K + LQ)(Q + E) \right)^{1/2}. \]
nodes.name: General large sieve
nodes.statement_short: Prop. 3.3 and Prop. 3.7 (with $S=1$) bound $\mathcal K_1$.

nodes.statement: Recalling that $\phi(h, h')$ is supported on $h, h' \asymp H$, we can bound $a_{e,q} \ll x^{o(1)} H$ by the divisor bound, and thus $\|a_{e,q}\|_2 \ll x^{o(1)} \sqrt{EQ} H$. The resulting bound for $\mathcal{K}_1$ is non-decreasing in $E, Q$, so we can plug this into \cref{eq:K-diag-split} to bound \[ \begin{aligned} \mathcal{K}(n = n') &\ll_{\varepsilon} x^{6\varepsilon} H \sqrt{THN} \left(L^2 TH N + \left(1 + \frac{K^2}{N^2}\right)^{\theta_{\max}} K (K + LN)(N + TH) \right)^{1/2} \\ &\ll x^{6\varepsilon} THN \left(\frac{L^2 H N}{T} + \frac{1}{T^2N}\left(1 + \frac{K^2}{N^2}\right)^{\theta_{\max}} K (K + LN)N^2 \right)^{1/2}, \end{aligned} \] where in the second line we multiplied and divided by $T$, then used the assumption $TH \ll N$. Since $\theta_{\max} \le 1/3$, we have \[ \frac{1}{T^2N}\left(1 + \frac{K^2}{N^2}\right)^{\theta_{\max}} \ll \left(1 + \frac{K^2}{N^5 T}\right)^{\theta_{\max}} \ll \left(1 + \frac{K^2}{N^3 TH^2}\right)^{\theta_{\max}}, \] so the contribution of $\mathcal{K}(n = n')$ is acceptable in \cref{eq:consequence-incomplete}.
nodes.name: Diagonal bound
nodes.statement_short: The diagonal contribution is acceptable.

nodes.statement:
To bound $\mathcal{K}(n 
eq n')$, we let $n_0 := (n, n')$, substitute $(n, n', e) \gets (n_0 n, n_0 n', n_0 e)$, and use the triangle inequality in $t$ to obtain \[ \mathcal{K}(n 
eq n') \ll \sum_{\substack{n_0 \le 2N \ n, n' \sim N/n_0 \ (n, n') = 1}} \sum_{\substack{1 \le |t| \le T \ t \mid n - n' 
eq 0}} \left\vert \sum_{\substack{h, h'\ e = at(n'h - nh') 
eq 0}} \phi(h, h') \sum_{\substack{k, \ell \ (k, dn_0nn'\ell) = 1}} \Phi\left( rac{\ell}{L},  rac{k}{K}ight) e\left( rac{e\overline{dn_0nn'\ell}}{k}ight) ight \vert. \]
nodes.name: Off-diagonal reduction
nodes.statement_short: Extract $n_0=(n,n')$ and use the triangle inequality in $t$.

nodes.statement: We then put $n_0$, $e \gets |e|$, and $q = dn_0 n n'$ in dyadic ranges, and use the divisor bound to write \begin{equation} \mathcal{K}(n \neq n') \ll x^{o(1)} \sup_{\substack{N_0 \ll N \\ E \ll |a| THN/N_0 \\ Q \asymp d N^2/N_0}} \mathcal{K}_2(N_0, E, Q), \end{equation} where \[ \begin{aligned} \mathcal{K}_2 &:= \sum_{q \sim Q} \max_{\substack{n_0 \le 2N \\ n, n' \sim N/n_0 \\ (n, n') = 1 \\ 1 \le |t| \le T}} \left \vert \sum_{e \sim E} \sum_{\substack{h, h' \\ at(n'h - nh') = \pm e}} \phi(h, h') \sum_{\substack{k, \ell \\ (k, q\ell) = 1}} \Phi_0\left(\frac{\ell}{L}\right) \Phi_0\left(\frac{k}{K}\right) e\left(\frac{\pm e \overline{q\ell}}{k}\right) \right \vert \\ &= \sum_{q \sim Q} \left \vert \sum_{e \sim E} a_{e,q} \sum_{\substack{k, \ell \\ (k, q\ell) = 1}} \Phi_0\left(\frac{\ell}{L}\right) \Phi_0\left(\frac{k}{K}\right) e\left(\frac{\pm e \overline{q\ell}}{k}\right) \right \vert. \end{aligned} \] Above, we denoted \[ a_{e,q} := \sum_{\substack{h, h' \in \mathbb{Z} \\ \pm at(q)(n'(q)h - n(q)h') = e}} \phi(h, h') \] if the maximum on the first line is attained at some $n(q), n'(q), t(q)$; if the maximum is empty, we let $a_{e,q} = 0$.
nodes.name: Define a_{e,q}
nodes.statement_short: Dyadic ranges and coefficients $a_{e,q}$ for the off-diagonal sum.

nodes.statement: \mathcal{K}(n \neq n') \ll x^{o(1)} \sup_{\substack{N_0 \ll N \\ E \ll |a| THN/N_0 \\ Q \asymp d N^2/N_0}} \mathcal{K}_2(N_0, E, Q),
nodes.name: Equation (6.4) eq:K-off-diag-split
nodes.label: eq:K-off-diag-split

nodes.statement: Then by \cref{prop:large-sieve-additive}, we know that $(q, E, x, (a_{e,q})_{e \sim E}, A_q, Y)$ satisfies \cref{ass:large-sieve}, where \[ Y := \frac{E H}{|a|(H+N/N_0)(N/N_0) \min_i T_H(\alpha_i)}, \quad A_q := \left(\sum_{e \sim E} |a_{e,q}|^2\right)^{1/2} + \sqrt{TE} \sqrt{\frac{H N_0}{N} + \frac{H^2 N_0^2}{N^2}}. \] Since $\min_i T_H(\alpha_i) \ll x^{2\varepsilon}$, we further have \[ Y \gg_\varepsilon x^{-2\varepsilon}\frac{E H N_0}{|a|(H+N)N}. \]
nodes.name: Additive large sieve
nodes.statement_short: Prop. 3.4 gives saving $Y$.

nodes.statement: From \cref{prop:kloosterman-incomplete}, we conclude that \[ \mathcal{K}_2 \ll_{\varepsilon,a} x^{2\varepsilon} \|A_q\|_2 \left(L^2 E Q + \left(1 + \frac{K^2}{Q^2 \frac{EHN_0}{(H+N)N}}\right)^{\theta_{\max}} K (K + LQ)(Q + E) \right)^{1/2}. \]
nodes.name: Incomplete Kloosterman bound
nodes.statement_short: Apply Prop. 3.7 to $\mathcal K_2$.

nodes.statement: Now by the same computation as in \cref{eq:primes-l2-bound} (incorporating a sum over $1 \le |t| \le T$, $t \mid e$), we have \[ \|A_q\|_2^2 \ll_\varepsilon x^{2\varepsilon} T E(HN + H^2 N_0), \] so that (using $|a| \le x^{\varepsilon}$) \[ \mathcal{K}_2 \ll_{\varepsilon} x^{4\varepsilon} \sqrt{T E(HN + H^2 N_0)} \left(L^2 E Q + \left(1 + \frac{K^2 (H+N)N}{Q^2 EHN_0}\right)^{\theta_{\max}} K (K + LQ)(Q + E) \right)^{1/2}. \]
nodes.name: l2 bound
nodes.statement_short: Bound $\|A_q\|_2$ as in (4.4).

nodes.statement: Since this right-hand side is non-decreasing in $E$ (due to $\theta_{\max} \le 1$), we may use the bounds $E \ll |a|THN/N_0$, $Q \asymp dN^2/N_0$ from \cref{eq:K-off-diag-split}, and $d \le x^{2\varepsilon}$ to obtain \[ \begin{aligned} &\mathcal{K}_2 \ll_{\varepsilon} x^{5\varepsilon} \sqrt{T \frac{THN}{N_0}(HN + H^2 N_0)} \\ &\times \left(L^2 \frac{THN}{N_0} \frac{N^2}{N_0} + \left(1 + \frac{K^2 (H+N)N}{\left(\frac{N^2}{N_0}\right)^2 \frac{THN}{N_0} HN_0}\right)^{\theta_{\max}} K \left(K + L\frac{N^2}{N_0}\right)\left(\frac{N^2}{N_0} + \frac{THN}{N_0}\right) \right)^{1/2}. \end{aligned} \] Since $\theta_{\max} \le 1/2$, this bound is seen to be non-increasing in the $N_0 \gg 1$ parameter; plugging this into \cref{eq:K-off-diag-split} and using the assumption $TH \ll N$, we conclude that \[ \begin{aligned} \mathcal{K}(n \neq n') \ll_{\varepsilon} x^{6\varepsilon} THN \left(L^2 TH N^3 + \left(1 + \frac{K^2}{N^3 TH^2}\right)^{\theta_{\max}} K \left(K + LN^2\right)N^2 \right)^{1/2}, \end{aligned} \] which gives the right-hand side of \cref{eq:consequence-incomplete}.
nodes.name: Optimize parameters
nodes.statement_short: Plug in extremal $E$, $Q$, $N_0$ to conclude.

nodes.statement: Let $\varepsilon > 0$ be small enough, $a \in \mathbb{Z} \setminus \{0\}$, $v, d_1, d_2 \in \mathbb{Z}_+$, $\theta := 7/32$, and $1 \ll M, K, N, L, H, R \ll x$ satisfy \begin{equation} \begin{gathered} |avd_1d_2| \ll x^\varepsilon, \qquad NL \ll x^\varepsilon K, \qquad R \ll K \ll \min(x^{-3\varepsilon} MN, LN^2), \qquad H \ll x^\varepsilon \frac{R}{M}, \\ K \ll x^{-25\varepsilon} \sqrt{M N R}, \qquad\quad K^{3+\theta} N^{2-3\theta} \ll x^{-200\varepsilon} M^{2-2\theta} R^{2+\theta} L. \end{gathered} \end{equation} Let $(u_k)_{K < k \le 4K}, (\beta_n)_{n \sim N}, (\lambda_\ell)_{\ell \sim L}$ be complex sequences such that $|u_k| \le \tau(k)$, $|\beta_n| \le 1$, $|\lambda_\ell| \le 1$, and \[ (k, vd_1d_2) > 1 \ \Rightarrow \ u_k = 0, \qquad\qquad (n\ell, vd_1) > 1 \ \Rightarrow \ \beta_n \lambda_\ell = 0. \] Then for any smooth functions $\Phi(t)$, $\Psi(t)$ supported in $t \asymp 1$ with $\Phi^{(j)}, \Psi^{(j)}, \ll_j 1$, and any $\omega \in \mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z}$ with $T_H(\omega) \ll x^\varepsilon$, one has \begin{equation} \begin{aligned} \sum_{\substack{r \sim R \\ (r, avd_1 d_2) = 1}} \frac{M}{r} \Psi\left(\frac{r}{R}\right) \sum_{\substack{k,n,\ell \\ d_1 k \equiv d_2 n\ell \pmod{r} \\ (d_1 k, d_2 n \ell) = 1}} u_k \beta_n \lambda_\ell \sum_{h \in \mathbb{Z}} e(h\omega)\, \Phi\left(\frac{h}{H}\right) e\left(\frac{-ha\overline{vd_1d_2k}}{r}\right) \\ \ll_{\varepsilon} x^{-10\varepsilon} \frac{KMNL}{R}. \end{aligned} \end{equation}
nodes.name: Exponential sum bound for convolutions
nodes.statement_short: Power-saving bound for the exponential sum from the first dispersion sum for triple convolutions, under the ranges (6.5).
assumptions: Let $\varepsilon > 0$ be small enough, $a \in \mathbb{Z} \setminus \{0\}$, $v, d_1, d_2 \in \mathbb{Z}_+$, $\theta := 7/32$, and $1 \ll M, K, N, L, H, R \ll x$ satisfy \begin{equation} \begin{gathered} |avd_1d_2| \ll x^\varepsilon, \qquad NL \ll x^\varepsilon K, \qquad R \ll K \ll \min(x^{-3\varepsilon} MN, LN^2), \qquad H \ll x^\varepsilon \frac{R}{M}, \\ K \ll x^{-25\varepsilon} \sqrt{M N R}, \qquad\quad K^{3+\theta} N^{2-3\theta} \ll x^{-200\varepsilon} M^{2-2\theta} R^{2+\theta} L. \end{gathered} \end{equation} Let $(u_k)_{K < k \le 4K}, (\beta_n)_{n \sim N}, (\lambda_\ell)_{\ell \sim L}$ be complex sequences such that $|u_k| \le \tau(k)$, $|\beta_n| \le 1$, $|\lambda_\ell| \le 1$, and \[ (k, vd_1d_2) > 1 \ \Rightarrow \ u_k = 0, \qquad\qquad (n\ell, vd_1) > 1 \ \Rightarrow \ \beta_n \lambda_\ell = 0. \]
conclusions: Then for any smooth functions $\Phi(t)$, $\Psi(t)$ supported in $t \asymp 1$ with $\Phi^{(j)}, \Psi^{(j)}, \ll_j 1$, and any $\omega \in \mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z}$ with $T_H(\omega) \ll x^\varepsilon$, one has \begin{equation} \begin{aligned} \sum_{\substack{r \sim R \\ (r, avd_1 d_2) = 1}} \frac{M}{r} \Psi\left(\frac{r}{R}\right) \sum_{\substack{k,n,\ell \\ d_1 k \equiv d_2 n\ell \pmod{r} \\ (d_1 k, d_2 n \ell) = 1}} u_k \beta_n \lambda_\ell \sum_{h \in \mathbb{Z}} e(h\omega)\, \Phi\left(\frac{h}{H}\right) e\left(\frac{-ha\overline{vd_1d_2k}}{r}\right) \\ \ll_{\varepsilon} x^{-10\varepsilon} \frac{KMNL}{R}. \end{aligned} \end{equation}
nodes.label: lem:expo-bound-convo

nodes.statement: \begin{gathered} |avd_1d_2| \ll x^\varepsilon, \qquad NL \ll x^\varepsilon K, \qquad R \ll K \ll \min(x^{-3\varepsilon} MN, LN^2), \qquad H \ll x^\varepsilon \frac{R}{M}, \\ K \ll x^{-25\varepsilon} \sqrt{M N R}, \qquad\quad K^{3+\theta} N^{2-3\theta} \ll x^{-200\varepsilon} M^{2-2\theta} R^{2+\theta} L. \end{gathered}
nodes.name: Ranges for the convolution exponential sum (6.5)
nodes.label: eq:expo-convo-ranges

nodes.statement: \begin{aligned} \sum_{\substack{r \sim R \\ (r, avd_1 d_2) = 1}} \frac{M}{r} \Psi\left(\frac{r}{R}\right) \sum_{\substack{k,n,\ell \\ d_1 k \equiv d_2 n\ell \pmod{r} \\ (d_1 k, d_2 n \ell) = 1}} u_k \beta_n \lambda_\ell \sum_{h \in \mathbb{Z}} e(h\omega)\, \Phi\left(\frac{h}{H}\right) e\left(\frac{-ha\overline{vd_1d_2k}}{r}\right) \\ \ll_{\varepsilon} x^{-10\varepsilon} \frac{KMNL}{R}. \end{aligned}
nodes.name: Exponential sum bound (6.6)
nodes.label: eq:expo-bound-convo

nodes.statement: As is common for exponential sum estimates with a variable $h \sim H$ coming from Poisson summation, \cref{lem:expo-bound-convo} needs to win a factor of $H$ (times an extra $x^\varepsilon$) over the trivial bound; the same was true for \cref{lem:expo-bound-well-fact}.
nodes.name: Winning a factor of H

nodes.statement:
We closely follow the proof of \cite[Proposition 1]{drappeau2015theoremes}. We denote the exponential sum considered in \cref{eq:expo-bound-convo} by $\mathcal{R}$; it is essentially identical to the sum in \cite[Section 3.5]{drappeau2015theoremes}, except that $h$ lies in a smooth dyadic range. As in \cite[Section 3.5]{drappeau2015theoremes}, we denote \[ 
u := vd_1 d_2 \ll x^\varepsilon \qquad\quad 	ext{and} \qquad\quad T :=  rac{\max(d_1 K, d_2 NL)}{R} \ll x^{2\varepsilon}  rac{K}{R}. \] Following through the computations in \cite[p.\,844--846]{drappeau2015theoremes} with minor changes, we obtain  egin{equation} \mathcal{R} \ll_\varepsilon x^{5\varepsilon} K M^{-1} + \max_{\substack{\sigma \mid a \ w \pmod{v}}} \left( x^{5\varepsilon} M R^{-1} (KLT)^{1/2} \mathcal{B}^{1/2} ight), \end{equation} where \[  egin{aligned} \mathcal{B} := \sum_{n, n' \sim N} \left \vert \sum_{\substack{1 \le |t| \le T \ (t, nn') = 1 \ t \mid n - n'}} \sum_{\ell} \Phi_0\left( rac{\ell}{L}ight) \sum_{(k, 
u d_2 nn'\ell) = 1} \Phi_0\left( rac{k}{K}ight) \sum_{h, h' \in \mathbb{Z}} \phi(h, h')\, e\left(a t (n'h - nh')  rac{\overline{
u d_2 nn'\ell}}{k}ight) ight \vert, \end{aligned} \] with \[ \phi(h, h') := \Phi\left( rac{h}{H}ight) \overline{\Phi\left( rac{h'}{H}ight)} e\left((h-h')\omega' ight), \qquad\quad \omega' := \omega +  rac{a \overline{w}}{v}. \] This corresponds to the sum on top of \cite[p.\,847]{drappeau2015theoremes}; note that we broke up the coefficients $ eta(n, h)$ in \cite[p.\,846]{drappeau2015theoremes} and ignored the phases in $n, n'$ via absolute values. We note at this point that by \cref{eq:tn}, \[  egin{aligned} T_H(\omega') &\le \min_{t \in \mathbb{Z}_+} \left(tv + H\|tv\omega'\|ight) \ &= \min_{t \in \mathbb{Z}_+} \left(tv + H\|tv\omega\|ight) \ &\le \min_{t \in \mathbb{Z}_+} v\left(t + H\|t\omega\|ight) = v T_H(\omega) \ll x^{2\varepsilon}. \end{aligned} \] Letting $e := at(n'h - nh')$, the contribution of $e = 0$ is bounded by \[ \mathcal{B}(e = 0) \ll_\varepsilon x^{\varepsilon} K L N H T, \] just as in \cite[(3.24)]{drappeau2015theoremes}. Since by \cref{eq:expo-convo-ranges}, \[ TH \ll x^{3\varepsilon}  rac{K}{R}  rac{R}{M} \ll x^{3\varepsilon}  rac{K}{M} \ll N, \] \cref{lem:consequence-incomplete} applies directly to the contribution of $e 
eq 0$, giving \[ \mathcal{B}(e 
eq 0) \ll_{\varepsilon} x^{6\varepsilon} THN \left(L^2 TH N^3 + \left(1 +  rac{K^2}{N^3 TH^2}ight)^	heta K \left(K + LN^2ight)N^2 ight)^{1/2}. \] Plugging these bounds and $K \le LN^2$ (from \cref{eq:expo-convo-ranges}) into \cref{eq:R-split}, we obtain \[  egin{aligned} \mathcal{R} &\ll_{\varepsilon} x^{5\varepsilon} K M^{-1} + x^{10\varepsilon} M R^{-1} \sqrt{KLT} \ &	imes \left(\sqrt{KLNHT} + \sqrt{THN} \left(L^2 TH N^3 + \left(1 +  rac{K^2}{N^3 TH^2}ight)^	heta K L N^4 ight)^{1/4}ight). \end{aligned} \] Combining $TH \ll N$ with $L \le NL \ll x^\varepsilon K$ (from \cref{eq:expo-convo-ranges}), we see that \[ L^2 T H N^3 \ll L^2 N^4 \ll x^\varepsilon KLN^4, \] so \[ \mathcal{R} \ll_{\varepsilon} x^{5\varepsilon} K M^{-1} + x^{11\varepsilon} M R^{-1} \sqrt{KLT} \left(\sqrt{KLNHT} + \sqrt{THN} \left(1 +  rac{K^2}{N^3 TH^2}ight)^{	heta/4} \left(K L N^4 ight)^{1/4} ight). \] Since this bound is non-decreasing in $H$ and $T$, we can plug in $H \le x^\varepsilon R/M$ (from \cref{eq:expo-convo-ranges}) and $T \le x^{2\varepsilon} K/R$ to obtain \[  egin{aligned} \mathcal{R} &\ll_{\varepsilon} x^{5\varepsilon} K M^{-1} + x^{15\varepsilon}  rac{M}{R} \sqrt{ rac{K^2L}{R}} \left(K\sqrt{ rac{LN}{M}} + \sqrt{ rac{KN}{M}} \left(1 +  rac{K M^2}{N^3 R}ight)^{	heta/4} \left(K L N^4 ight)^{1/4}ight) \ &= x^{5\varepsilon} K M^{-1} + x^{15\varepsilon}  rac{K^2 L \sqrt{MN}}{R^{3/2}} + x^{15\varepsilon}  rac{K^{7/4} L^{3/4} M^{1/2} N^{3/2}}{R^{3/2}} \left(1 +  rac{K M^2}{N^3 R}ight)^{	heta/4}. \end{aligned} \] This is acceptable in \cref{eq:expo-bound-convo} (i.e., $\ll_{\varepsilon} x^{-10\varepsilon} KMNL/R$) provided that \[  egin{gathered} R \ll x^{-15\varepsilon} M^2 N L, \qquad\qquad K \ll x^{-25\varepsilon} \sqrt{M N R}, \ K^{3} N^{2} \ll x^{-100\varepsilon} M^2 R^2 L, \qquad\qquad K^{3+	heta} N^{2-3	heta} \ll x^{-100\varepsilon} M^{2-2	heta} R^{2+	heta} L. \end{gathered} \] The first of these conditions follows easily from $R \ll K \ll x^{-25\varepsilon} \sqrt{MNR}$, while the second and fourth conditions are part of \cref{eq:expo-convo-ranges}. It remains to verify the third condition which can be deduced from \cref{eq:expo-convo-ranges} as follows: \[  egin{aligned} K^3 N^2 = \left(K^{3-3	heta} N^{2-2	heta}ight)^{ rac{1}{1-	heta}} &\ll \left(\left( rac{K}{R}ight)^{3	heta} \left( rac{x^\varepsilon K}{NL}ight)^{	heta} K^{3-3	heta} N^{2-2	heta}ight)^{ rac{1}{1-	heta}} \ &= \left(  rac{x^{	heta\varepsilon}}{R^{3	heta} L^	heta} K^{3+	heta} N^{2-3	heta}ight)^{ rac{1}{1-	heta}} \ &\ll \left(  rac{1}{R^{3	heta} L^	heta} x^{(	heta-200)\varepsilon} M^{2-2	heta} R^{2+	heta} Light)^{ rac{1}{1-	heta}} \ &\ll x^{-100\varepsilon} \left(M^{2-2	heta} R^{2-2	heta} L^{1-	heta} ight)^{ rac{1}{1-	heta}} = x^{-100\varepsilon} M^2 R^2 L. \end{aligned} \] This completes our proof.
nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 6.2
nodes.statement_short: Follow Drappeau's Proposition 1 to reduce to a sum $\mathcal B$, then bound it with Lemma 6.1. Key step: checking the resulting range conditions.

nodes.statement: We closely follow the proof of \cite[Proposition 1]{drappeau2015theoremes}. We denote the exponential sum considered in \cref{eq:expo-bound-convo} by $\mathcal{R}$; it is essentially identical to the sum in \cite[Section 3.5]{drappeau2015theoremes}, except that $h$ lies in a smooth dyadic range.
nodes.name: Follow Drappeau
nodes.statement_short: Follow Drappeau's Proposition 1.

nodes.statement: As in \cite[Section 3.5]{drappeau2015theoremes}, we denote \[ \nu := vd_1 d_2 \ll x^\varepsilon \qquad\quad \text{and} \qquad\quad T := \frac{\max(d_1 K, d_2 NL)}{R} \ll x^{2\varepsilon} \frac{K}{R}. \]
nodes.name: Introduce nu, T
nodes.statement_short: Introduce $\nu$ and $T$.

nodes.statement: Following through the computations in \cite[p.\,844--846]{drappeau2015theoremes} with minor changes, we obtain \begin{equation} \mathcal{R} \ll_\varepsilon x^{5\varepsilon} K M^{-1} + \max_{\substack{\sigma \mid a \\ w \pmod{v}}} \left( x^{5\varepsilon} M R^{-1} (KLT)^{1/2} \mathcal{B}^{1/2} \right), \end{equation} where \[ \begin{aligned} \mathcal{B} := \sum_{n, n' \sim N} \left \vert \sum_{\substack{1 \le |t| \le T \\ (t, nn') = 1 \\ t \mid n - n'}} \sum_{\ell} \Phi_0\left(\frac{\ell}{L}\right) \sum_{(k, \nu d_2 nn'\ell) = 1} \Phi_0\left(\frac{k}{K}\right) \sum_{h, h' \in \mathbb{Z}} \phi(h, h')\, e\left(a t (n'h - nh') \frac{\overline{\nu d_2 nn'\ell}}{k}\right) \right \vert, \end{aligned} \] with \[ \phi(h, h') := \Phi\left(\frac{h}{H}\right) \overline{\Phi\left(\frac{h'}{H}\right)} e\left((h-h')\omega' \right), \qquad\quad \omega' := \omega + \frac{a \overline{w}}{v}. \] This corresponds to the sum on top of \cite[p.\,847]{drappeau2015theoremes}; note that we broke up the coefficients $\beta(n, h)$ in \cite[p.\,846]{drappeau2015theoremes} and ignored the phases in $n, n'$ via absolute values.
nodes.name: Reduce to B
nodes.statement_short: Drappeau's computations reduce $\mathcal R$ to $\mathcal B$.

nodes.statement: \mathcal{R} \ll_\varepsilon x^{5\varepsilon} K M^{-1} + \max_{\substack{\sigma \mid a \\ w \pmod{v}}} \left( x^{5\varepsilon} M R^{-1} (KLT)^{1/2} \mathcal{B}^{1/2} \right),
nodes.name: Equation (6.7) eq:R-split
nodes.label: eq:R-split

nodes.statement: We note at this point that by \cref{eq:tn}, \[ \begin{aligned} T_H(\omega') &\le \min_{t \in \mathbb{Z}_+} \left(tv + H\|tv\omega'\|\right) \\ &= \min_{t \in \mathbb{Z}_+} \left(tv + H\|tv\omega\|\right) \\ &\le \min_{t \in \mathbb{Z}_+} v\left(t + H\|t\omega\|\right) = v T_H(\omega) \ll x^{2\varepsilon}. \end{aligned} \]
nodes.name: Bound T_H(omega')
nodes.statement_short: $T_H(\omega')\le vT_H(\omega)$.

nodes.statement: Letting $e := at(n'h - nh')$, the contribution of $e = 0$ is bounded by \[ \mathcal{B}(e = 0) \ll_\varepsilon x^{\varepsilon} K L N H T, \] just as in \cite[(3.24)]{drappeau2015theoremes}.
nodes.name: e = 0 terms
nodes.statement_short: Bound the $e=0$ contribution.

nodes.statement: Since by \cref{eq:expo-convo-ranges}, \[ TH \ll x^{3\varepsilon} \frac{K}{R} \frac{R}{M} \ll x^{3\varepsilon} \frac{K}{M} \ll N, \] \cref{lem:consequence-incomplete} applies directly to the contribution of $e \neq 0$, giving \[ \mathcal{B}(e \neq 0) \ll_{\varepsilon} x^{6\varepsilon} THN \left(L^2 TH N^3 + \left(1 + \frac{K^2}{N^3 TH^2}\right)^\theta K \left(K + LN^2\right)N^2 \right)^{1/2}. \]
nodes.name: Apply Lemma 6.1
nodes.statement_short: Lemma 6.1 bounds the $e\neq0$ contribution.

nodes.statement: Plugging these bounds and $K \le LN^2$ (from \cref{eq:expo-convo-ranges}) into \cref{eq:R-split}, we obtain \[ \begin{aligned} \mathcal{R} &\ll_{\varepsilon} x^{5\varepsilon} K M^{-1} + x^{10\varepsilon} M R^{-1} \sqrt{KLT} \\ &\times \left(\sqrt{KLNHT} + \sqrt{THN} \left(L^2 TH N^3 + \left(1 + \frac{K^2}{N^3 TH^2}\right)^\theta K L N^4 \right)^{1/4}\right). \end{aligned} \]
nodes.name: Combine bounds
nodes.statement_short: Insert the bounds into (6.7).

nodes.statement: Combining $TH \ll N$ with $L \le NL \ll x^\varepsilon K$ (from \cref{eq:expo-convo-ranges}), we see that \[ L^2 T H N^3 \ll L^2 N^4 \ll x^\varepsilon KLN^4, \] so \[ \mathcal{R} \ll_{\varepsilon} x^{5\varepsilon} K M^{-1} + x^{11\varepsilon} M R^{-1} \sqrt{KLT} \left(\sqrt{KLNHT} + \sqrt{THN} \left(1 + \frac{K^2}{N^3 TH^2}\right)^{\theta/4} \left(K L N^4 \right)^{1/4} \right). \]
nodes.name: Simplify
nodes.statement_short: Drop the term $L^2THN^3$.

nodes.statement: Since this bound is non-decreasing in $H$ and $T$, we can plug in $H \le x^\varepsilon R/M$ (from \cref{eq:expo-convo-ranges}) and $T \le x^{2\varepsilon} K/R$ to obtain \[ \begin{aligned} \mathcal{R} &\ll_{\varepsilon} x^{5\varepsilon} K M^{-1} + x^{15\varepsilon} \frac{M}{R} \sqrt{\frac{K^2L}{R}} \left(K\sqrt{\frac{LN}{M}} + \sqrt{\frac{KN}{M}} \left(1 + \frac{K M^2}{N^3 R}\right)^{\theta/4} \left(K L N^4 \right)^{1/4}\right) \\ &= x^{5\varepsilon} K M^{-1} + x^{15\varepsilon} \frac{K^2 L \sqrt{MN}}{R^{3/2}} + x^{15\varepsilon} \frac{K^{7/4} L^{3/4} M^{1/2} N^{3/2}}{R^{3/2}} \left(1 + \frac{K M^2}{N^3 R}\right)^{\theta/4}. \end{aligned} \]
nodes.name: Plug in H and T
nodes.statement_short: Insert the maximal $H$ and $T$.

nodes.statement: This is acceptable in \cref{eq:expo-bound-convo} (i.e., $\ll_{\varepsilon} x^{-10\varepsilon} KMNL/R$) provided that \[ \begin{gathered} R \ll x^{-15\varepsilon} M^2 N L, \qquad\qquad K \ll x^{-25\varepsilon} \sqrt{M N R}, \\ K^{3} N^{2} \ll x^{-100\varepsilon} M^2 R^2 L, \qquad\qquad K^{3+\theta} N^{2-3\theta} \ll x^{-100\varepsilon} M^{2-2\theta} R^{2+\theta} L. \end{gathered} \] The first of these conditions follows easily from $R \ll K \ll x^{-25\varepsilon} \sqrt{MNR}$, while the second and fourth conditions are part of \cref{eq:expo-convo-ranges}.
nodes.name: Acceptability conditions
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to four range conditions.

nodes.statement: It remains to verify the third condition which can be deduced from \cref{eq:expo-convo-ranges} as follows: \[ \begin{aligned} K^3 N^2 = \left(K^{3-3\theta} N^{2-2\theta}\right)^{\frac{1}{1-\theta}} &\ll \left(\left(\frac{K}{R}\right)^{3\theta} \left(\frac{x^\varepsilon K}{NL}\right)^{\theta} K^{3-3\theta} N^{2-2\theta}\right)^{\frac{1}{1-\theta}} \\ &= \left( \frac{x^{\theta\varepsilon}}{R^{3\theta} L^\theta} K^{3+\theta} N^{2-3\theta}\right)^{\frac{1}{1-\theta}} \\ &\ll \left( \frac{1}{R^{3\theta} L^\theta} x^{(\theta-200)\varepsilon} M^{2-2\theta} R^{2+\theta} L\right)^{\frac{1}{1-\theta}} \\ &\ll x^{-100\varepsilon} \left(M^{2-2\theta} R^{2-2\theta} L^{1-\theta} \right)^{\frac{1}{1-\theta}} = x^{-100\varepsilon} M^2 R^2 L. \end{aligned} \] This completes our proof.
nodes.name: Verify third condition
nodes.statement_short: Derive the third condition from (6.5) by interpolation.

nodes.statement: For $r \in \mathbb{Z}_+$ and $k \pmod{r}$, we recall Drappeau's notation \begin{equation} \omega_\varepsilon(k; r) := \sum_{\substack{\chi \text{ primitive} \\ \textnormal{cond}(\chi) \le x^\varepsilon \\ \textnormal{cond}(\chi) \mid r}} \chi(k) \end{equation} from \cite[(3.1)]{drappeau2015theoremes}.
nodes.name: Small-conductor character sum omega

nodes.statement: \omega_\varepsilon(k; r) := \sum_{\substack{\chi \text{ primitive} \\ \textnormal{cond}(\chi) \le x^\varepsilon \\ \textnormal{cond}(\chi) \mid r}} \chi(k)
nodes.name: Definition of omega_epsilon (6.8)
nodes.label: eq:small-cond-chars

nodes.statement: For any small enough $\varepsilon > 0$, there exists $\delta > 0$ such that the following holds. Let $M, N, L \gg 1$, $x := MNL$, $a_1, a_2 \in \mathbb{Z} \setminus \{0\}$ satisfy $|a_1a_2| \le x^\delta$, $(a_1, a_2) = 1$, and $(\alpha_m)_{m \sim M}, (\beta_n)_{n \sim N}, (\gamma_\ell)_{\ell\sim L}$ be $1$-bounded complex sequences. Suppose that with $\theta := 7/32$, one has \begin{equation} \begin{gathered} x^\varepsilon \le N, \qquad NL \le x^{2/3-5\varepsilon}, \qquad L \le x^{-\varepsilon} M, \qquad M \le R \le x^{-\varepsilon} NL, \qquad N^2 L^3 \le x^{1-\varepsilon} R, \\ N^{7-4\theta} L^{4-\theta} \le x^{2-2\theta-\varepsilon} R^{2+\theta}. \end{gathered} \end{equation} Then one has \[ \sum_{\substack{r \sim R \\ (r, a_1 a_2) = 1}} \left\vert \sum_{\substack{m \sim M \\ n \sim N \\ \ell \sim L}} \alpha_m \beta_n \gamma_\ell \left(\mathbbm{1}_{mn\ell \equiv a_1 \overline{a_2} \pmod{r}} - \frac{\mathbbm{1}_{(mn\ell, r) = 1}}{\varphi(r)} \omega_\varepsilon(mn\ell \overline{a_1} a_2; r) \right) \right\vert \ll_{\varepsilon,a_1,a_2} x^{1-\delta}. \]
nodes.name: Triple convolution estimate
nodes.statement_short: Power-saving equidistribution of triple convolutions $\alpha*\beta*\gamma$ in APs to moduli $r\sim R$ (after removing small-conductor characters) in the ranges (6.9).
assumptions: For any small enough $\varepsilon > 0$, there exists $\delta > 0$ such that the following holds. Let $M, N, L \gg 1$, $x := MNL$, $a_1, a_2 \in \mathbb{Z} \setminus \{0\}$ satisfy $|a_1a_2| \le x^\delta$, $(a_1, a_2) = 1$, and $(\alpha_m)_{m \sim M}, (\beta_n)_{n \sim N}, (\gamma_\ell)_{\ell\sim L}$ be $1$-bounded complex sequences. Suppose that with $\theta := 7/32$, one has \begin{equation} \begin{gathered} x^\varepsilon \le N, \qquad NL \le x^{2/3-5\varepsilon}, \qquad L \le x^{-\varepsilon} M, \qquad M \le R \le x^{-\varepsilon} NL, \qquad N^2 L^3 \le x^{1-\varepsilon} R, \\ N^{7-4\theta} L^{4-\theta} \le x^{2-2\theta-\varepsilon} R^{2+\theta}. \end{gathered} \end{equation}
conclusions: Then one has \[ \sum_{\substack{r \sim R \\ (r, a_1 a_2) = 1}} \left\vert \sum_{\substack{m \sim M \\ n \sim N \\ \ell \sim L}} \alpha_m \beta_n \gamma_\ell \left(\mathbbm{1}_{mn\ell \equiv a_1 \overline{a_2} \pmod{r}} - \frac{\mathbbm{1}_{(mn\ell, r) = 1}}{\varphi(r)} \omega_\varepsilon(mn\ell \overline{a_1} a_2; r) \right) \right\vert \ll_{\varepsilon,a_1,a_2} x^{1-\delta}. \]
nodes.label: prop:triple-convo

nodes.statement: \begin{gathered} x^\varepsilon \le N, \qquad NL \le x^{2/3-5\varepsilon}, \qquad L \le x^{-\varepsilon} M, \qquad M \le R \le x^{-\varepsilon} NL, \qquad N^2 L^3 \le x^{1-\varepsilon} R, \\ N^{7-4\theta} L^{4-\theta} \le x^{2-2\theta-\varepsilon} R^{2+\theta}. \end{gathered}
nodes.name: Ranges for the triple convolution estimate (6.9)
nodes.label: eq:triple-convo-ranges

nodes.statement: The inequalities $R \le x^{-o(1)} NL$, $N^2 L^3 \le x^{1-o(1)} R$, and $N^{7-4\theta} L^{4-\theta} \le x^{2-2\theta-o(1)} R^{2+\theta}$ imply $R \le x^{5/8 - o(1)}$, which corresponds to the level from \cref{thm:smooth}. We note that for $R = x^{-o(1)} NL$, the last inequality in \cref{eq:triple-convo-ranges} is equivalent to $N^7 L^4 \le x^{-o(1)} R^2$, which explains why our final exponent of distribution does not depend on the $\theta$ parameter.
nodes.name: Level 5/8 from the triple convolution ranges

nodes.statement: We closely follow the proof of \cite[Th\'ero\`eme 3]{drappeau2015theoremes}, which applies Cauchy--Schwarz in $r, m$ (and inserts a smooth majorant $f(m) = \Phi(m/M)$) to obtain three dispersion sums \cite[Section 3.1]{drappeau2015theoremes}. We change nothing in the treatment of the second and third dispersion sums from \cite[Sections 3.2, 3.3]{drappeau2015theoremes}, noting that the conditions on the top row of \cref{eq:triple-convo-ranges} are sufficient here. We also begin treating the first dispersion sum similarly as in \cite[Section 3.4]{drappeau2015theoremes}, with the technical change that we Poisson complete via \cref{lem:truncated-poisson} rather than \cite[Lemme 2]{drappeau2015theoremes}. Instead of \cite[(3.12)]{drappeau2015theoremes}, we thus obtain \[ \mathcal{S}_1 = \widehat{f}(0)X_1 + \sum_{\substack{v, d_1,e_1,e_2 \le x^\eta \\ d_1 \mid v^\infty, e_1 \mid a_2^\infty, e_2 \mid a_2}} \int_{0.1}^{10} \sum_{\substack{H_j = 2^j \\ 1 \le H_j \le H}} R_{j,u}(v; d_1, e_1, e_2)\, \frac{du}{u} + O_\eta(x^{1-\eta/4} K R^{-1}), \] where $X_1$ is the main term from \cite[(3.12)]{drappeau2015theoremes}, $H = x^\eta R M^{-1}$, $\Psi_j$ are as in \cref{lem:truncated-poisson}, and \[ R_{j,u}(v; d_1, e_1, e_2) := \sum_{\substack{r \sim R \\ (r, a_1a_2v) = 1}} \frac{M}{r} \widetilde\Phi\left(\frac{ur}{R}\right) \sum_{(k_1, k_2) \in \mathcal{K}} u_{k_1} \overline{u_{k_2}} \sum_{h \in \mathbb{Z}} e\left(h\omega\right) \Psi_j\left(\frac{|h|}{H_j}\right) e\left(\frac{-ha_1\overline{a_2k_1}}{r}\right), \] where $u_k := \sum_{n\ell = k} \beta_n \gamma_\ell$, $\mathcal{K}$ is as in \cite[p.\,841]{drappeau2015theoremes}, and \[ \omega := \frac{uM}{R} \ll H^{-1} x^\eta \qquad\quad \Rightarrow \qquad\quad T_H(\omega) \ll x^\eta. \] We then develop and bound $R_{j,u}$ as in \cite[p.\,843]{drappeau2015theoremes}, with the only major change that we use our \cref{lem:expo-bound-convo} instead of \cite[Proposition 1]{drappeau2015theoremes}. To apply \cref{lem:expo-bound-convo} (with $\eta > 0$ in place of $\varepsilon$), we need to verify the conditions in \cref{eq:expo-convo-ranges}; thus instead of the third-to-last display on \cite[p.\,843]{drappeau2015theoremes}, we require that $|a_1 a_2| \le x^{\eta/10}$ and \[ \begin{gathered} R \ll x^{-100\eta} NL, \qquad\quad L \ll x^{-100\eta} M, \qquad\quad 1 \ll x^{-100\eta} N, \\ \sqrt{N} L \ll x^{-200\eta} \sqrt{M R}, \qquad\quad N^{5-2\theta} L^{2+\theta} \ll x^{-300\eta} M^{2-2\theta} R^{2+\theta}. \end{gathered} \] Here, we implicitly used that in Drappeau's computations near \cite[bottom of p.\,843]{drappeau2015theoremes}, one has $vd_1d_2 \ll x^{5\eta}$, $H = x^\eta R M^{-1}$, and $x^{10\eta} NL \ll K \ll x^{-10\eta} NL$. Since $MNL \asymp x$, these conditions follow from \cref{eq:triple-convo-ranges} provided $\eta$ is chosen sufficiently small in terms of $\varepsilon$.
nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 6.3
nodes.statement_short: Follow Drappeau's Théorème 3, replacing the first dispersion sum's exponential sum bound by Lemma 6.2.

nodes.statement: We closely follow the proof of \cite[Th\'ero\`eme 3]{drappeau2015theoremes}, which applies Cauchy--Schwarz in $r, m$ (and inserts a smooth majorant $f(m) = \Phi(m/M)$) to obtain three dispersion sums \cite[Section 3.1]{drappeau2015theoremes}. We change nothing in the treatment of the second and third dispersion sums from \cite[Sections 3.2, 3.3]{drappeau2015theoremes}, noting that the conditions on the top row of \cref{eq:triple-convo-ranges} are sufficient here.
nodes.name: Follow Drappeau Théorème 3
nodes.statement_short: Second and third dispersion sums as in Drappeau.

nodes.statement: We also begin treating the first dispersion sum similarly as in \cite[Section 3.4]{drappeau2015theoremes}, with the technical change that we Poisson complete via \cref{lem:truncated-poisson} rather than \cite[Lemme 2]{drappeau2015theoremes}. Instead of \cite[(3.12)]{drappeau2015theoremes}, we thus obtain \[ \mathcal{S}_1 = \widehat{f}(0)X_1 + \sum_{\substack{v, d_1,e_1,e_2 \le x^\eta \\ d_1 \mid v^\infty, e_1 \mid a_2^\infty, e_2 \mid a_2}} \int_{0.1}^{10} \sum_{\substack{H_j = 2^j \\ 1 \le H_j \le H}} R_{j,u}(v; d_1, e_1, e_2)\, \frac{du}{u} + O_\eta(x^{1-\eta/4} K R^{-1}), \] where $X_1$ is the main term from \cite[(3.12)]{drappeau2015theoremes}, $H = x^\eta R M^{-1}$, $\Psi_j$ are as in \cref{lem:truncated-poisson}, and \[ R_{j,u}(v; d_1, e_1, e_2) := \sum_{\substack{r \sim R \\ (r, a_1a_2v) = 1}} \frac{M}{r} \widetilde\Phi\left(\frac{ur}{R}\right) \sum_{(k_1, k_2) \in \mathcal{K}} u_{k_1} \overline{u_{k_2}} \sum_{h \in \mathbb{Z}} e\left(h\omega\right) \Psi_j\left(\frac{|h|}{H_j}\right) e\left(\frac{-ha_1\overline{a_2k_1}}{r}\right), \] where $u_k := \sum_{n\ell = k} \beta_n \gamma_\ell$, $\mathcal{K}$ is as in \cite[p.\,841]{drappeau2015theoremes}, and \[ \omega := \frac{uM}{R} \ll H^{-1} x^\eta \qquad\quad \Rightarrow \qquad\quad T_H(\omega) \ll x^\eta. \]
nodes.name: Poisson completion
nodes.statement_short: Complete via Lemma 3.1, obtaining the sums $R_{j,u}$.

nodes.statement: We then develop and bound $R_{j,u}$ as in \cite[p.\,843]{drappeau2015theoremes}, with the only major change that we use our \cref{lem:expo-bound-convo} instead of \cite[Proposition 1]{drappeau2015theoremes}. To apply \cref{lem:expo-bound-convo} (with $\eta > 0$ in place of $\varepsilon$), we need to verify the conditions in \cref{eq:expo-convo-ranges}; thus instead of the third-to-last display on \cite[p.\,843]{drappeau2015theoremes}, we require that $|a_1 a_2| \le x^{\eta/10}$ and \[ \begin{gathered} R \ll x^{-100\eta} NL, \qquad\quad L \ll x^{-100\eta} M, \qquad\quad 1 \ll x^{-100\eta} N, \\ \sqrt{N} L \ll x^{-200\eta} \sqrt{M R}, \qquad\quad N^{5-2\theta} L^{2+\theta} \ll x^{-300\eta} M^{2-2\theta} R^{2+\theta}. \end{gathered} \]
nodes.name: Apply Lemma 6.2
nodes.statement_short: Bound $R_{j,u}$ via Lemma 6.2 under range conditions.

nodes.statement: Here, we implicitly used that in Drappeau's computations near \cite[bottom of p.\,843]{drappeau2015theoremes}, one has $vd_1d_2 \ll x^{5\eta}$, $H = x^\eta R M^{-1}$, and $x^{10\eta} NL \ll K \ll x^{-10\eta} NL$. Since $MNL \asymp x$, these conditions follow from \cref{eq:triple-convo-ranges} provided $\eta$ is chosen sufficiently small in terms of $\varepsilon$.
nodes.name: Check ranges
nodes.statement_short: The conditions follow from (6.9).

nodes.statement: We recall the notation specific to smooth numbers, \[ u := \frac{\log x}{\log y}, \qquad\quad H(u) := \exp\left(\frac{u}{(\log (u+1))^2}\right), \] from \cite{drappeau2015theoremes}, as well as the definitions of $\Psi_q(x, y)$ and $\Psi(x, y; a, q)$ from \cref{eq:smooth-notations}.
nodes.name: Smooth number parameters u and H(u)

nodes.statement: For any $\varepsilon > 0$, there exist $\delta, C > 0$ such that the following holds. Let $x \ge 2$ and $a_1, a_2 \in \mathbb{Z} \setminus \{0\}$ satisfy $(a_1, a_2) = 1$ and $|a_1a_2| \le x^\delta$. Then for any $y \in [(\log x)^C, x^{1/C}]$ and $A \ge 0$, one has \[ \sum_{\substack{q \le x^{5/8-\varepsilon} \\ (q, a_1 a_2) = 1}} \left\vert \Psi(x, y; a_1 \overline{a_2}, q) - \frac{\Psi_q(x, y)}{\varphi(q)} \right\vert \ll_{\varepsilon,A} \Psi(x, y)\left( H(u)^{-\delta} (\log x)^{-A} + y^{-\delta} \right). \] The implicit constant is effective if $A < 1$.
nodes.name: Smooth numbers in APs to large moduli, refined
nodes.statement_short: Refined version of the smooth-number equidistribution to moduli $x^{5/8-\varepsilon}$, with saving $H(u)^{-\delta}(\log x)^{-A}+y^{-\delta}$.
assumptions: For any $\varepsilon > 0$, there exist $\delta, C > 0$ such that the following holds. Let $x \ge 2$ and $a_1, a_2 \in \mathbb{Z} \setminus \{0\}$ satisfy $(a_1, a_2) = 1$ and $|a_1a_2| \le x^\delta$.
conclusions: Then for any $y \in [(\log x)^C, x^{1/C}]$ and $A \ge 0$, one has \[ \sum_{\substack{q \le x^{5/8-\varepsilon} \\ (q, a_1 a_2) = 1}} \left\vert \Psi(x, y; a_1 \overline{a_2}, q) - \frac{\Psi_q(x, y)}{\varphi(q)} \right\vert \ll_{\varepsilon,A} \Psi(x, y)\left( H(u)^{-\delta} (\log x)^{-A} + y^{-\delta} \right). \] The implicit constant is effective if $A < 1$.
nodes.label: thm:smooth-refined

nodes.statement: We assume without loss of generality that $\varepsilon > 0$ is small enough, and choose $\eta$ to be a small multiple of $\varepsilon$. As in \cite[p.\,855--856]{drappeau2015theoremes}, Harper's result \cite[Lemme 5]{drappeau2015theoremes} (see also \cite{harper2012bombieri}) handles the contribution of Dirichlet characters with conductors $\le x^\eta$, so it suffices to prove the bound \begin{equation} \sum_{\substack{q \le x^{5/8-\varepsilon} \\ (q, a_1 a_2) = 1}} \left\vert \sum_{\substack{n \le x \\ P^+(n) \le y}} \left(\mathbbm{1}_{n \equiv a_1 \overline{a_2} \pmod{q}} - \frac{\mathbbm{1}_{(n, q) = 1}}{\varphi(q)} \omega_\eta(n; a_1\overline{a_2})\right) \right\vert \ll_\varepsilon x^{1-\delta/2}, \end{equation} for some $\delta = \delta(\varepsilon) > 0$. Such a power-saving is enough up to a final rescaling of $\delta$, due to the bound $x^{1-\delta/2} \ll_\delta \Psi(x, y) y^{-\delta/4}$ for sufficiently large $C$ (see \cite[p.\,856]{drappeau2015theoremes}). The proof of \cref{eq:smooth-power-saving} is completely analogous to that of \cite[Proposition 2]{drappeau2015theoremes}, except that we use our triple convolution estimate from \cref{prop:triple-convo} instead of \cite[Th\'eor\`eme 3]{drappeau2015theoremes}. The key point is that the indicator function of smooth numbers can be approximated by convolutions of three sequences with pre-specified ranges, due to their flexible factorization. Specifically, we rescale $\varepsilon \gets 100\varepsilon$, take $C = \varepsilon^{-1}$ so that $y \le x^{1/C} \le x^\varepsilon$, and put $q \gets r$ in dyadic ranges $r \sim R$. Then instead of the parameters on the bottom of \cite[p.\,852]{drappeau2015theoremes}, we pick \[ M_0 := \frac{x^{1-10\varepsilon}}{R}, \qquad\quad N_0 := \frac{R^2}{x^{1-40\varepsilon}}, \qquad\quad L_0 := \frac{x^{1-30\varepsilon}}{R}, \] in the range $x^{(1/2) - (\varepsilon/10)} \le R \le x^{5/8-100\varepsilon}$ (smaller values of $R$ are covered by previous results \cite{drappeau2015theoremes}). Any resulting values of $M, N, L$ with \[ M_0 \le M \le y \frac{M_0}{2}, \qquad\quad L_0 \le L \le y \frac{L_0}{2}, \qquad\quad y^{-2} N_0 \le N \le N_0 \] are seen to satisfy the conditions in \cref{eq:triple-convo-ranges}. In particular, for the last two conditions in \cref{eq:triple-convo-ranges}, we note that \[ \frac{x R}{N_0^2 L_0^3} = x^{10\varepsilon} \qquad\quad \text{and} \qquad\quad \frac{x^{2-2\theta} R^{2+\theta}}{N_0^{7-4\theta} L_0^{4-\theta}} = \frac{x^{5(1-\theta)-(160-130\theta)\varepsilon}}{R^{8(1-\theta)}} \ge x^{100\varepsilon}, \] since $R \le x^{5/8-100\varepsilon}$; this gives enough $x^{o(1)}$ room when replacing $M_0, N_0, L_0$ by $M, N, L$, since $y \le x^\varepsilon$. Following through the combinatorial decompositions and separations of variables in \cite[p.\,852--854]{drappeau2015theoremes}, we can apply \cref{prop:triple-convo} for the sequences $(\alpha_m)^{(j)}, (\beta_m)^{(j)}, (\lambda_\ell)^{(j)}$ on \cite[p.\,854]{drappeau2015theoremes}, which recovers the desired bound.

nodes.statement_short: Remove small conductors via Harper's result, then approximate smooth numbers by triple convolutions with chosen ranges and apply Proposition 6.3.

nodes.statement: For any $\varepsilon, A > 0$ and $k \ge 1$, there exist $\delta, C > 0$ such that the following holds. Let $x \ge 2$ and $a_1, a_2 \in \mathbb{Z}\setminus \{0\}$ satisfy $(a_1, a_2) = 1$ and $|a_1a_2| \le x^\delta$. Then for any $y_1 \in [(\log x)^C, x^{1/C}]$, $y_2 \in [(\log x)^C, x]$, $Q \le x^{5/8 - \varepsilon}$, and $q_0 \in \mathbb{Z}_+$ with $q_0 \le x^\delta$, $(q_0, a_1a_2) = 1$, $P^+(q_0) \le y_2$, one has \begin{equation} \sum_{\substack{q \sim Q \\ P^+(q) \le y_2 \\ (q, a_1a_2) = 1}} \tau_k(q) \left\vert \Psi(x, y_1; a_1\overline{a_2}, q_0q) - \frac{\Psi_{q_0q}(x, y_1)}{\varphi(q_0q)} \right\vert \ll_{\varepsilon,A,k} \frac{\Psi(x, y_1)}{(\log x)^A} \frac{\Psi(Q, y_2)}{\varphi(q_0)Q} e^{O_k(u_2)}, \end{equation} where $u_2 := (\log x)/\log y_2$.

nodes.statement_short: Smooth numbers are equidistributed in APs on average over smooth moduli up to $x^{5/8-\varepsilon}$, weighted by $\tau_k$.

nodes.statement: Again, we assume without loss of generality that $\varepsilon > 0$ is small enough, and we will pick $\eta, \delta$ to be small enough in terms of $\varepsilon, A, k$. It suffices to prove our claim with $\delta$ replaced by $\delta/10$. Let $\mathcal{S}$ denote the left-hand side of \cref{eq:smooth-mod-smooth}. Recalling the notation in \cref{eq:small-cond-chars}, we separate the contribution of Dirichlet characters of small conductors by writing \[ |\mathcal{S}| \le \mathcal{S}_{\text{small}} + \mathcal{S}_{\text{large}}, \] where \[ \begin{aligned} \mathcal{S}_{\text{large}} &:= \sum_{\substack{q \sim Q \\ P^+(q) \le y_2 \\ (q, a_1a_2) = 1}} \tau_k(q) \left\vert \sum_{\substack{n \le x \\ P^+(n) \le y_1}} \left(\mathbbm{1}_{n \equiv a_1\overline{a_2} \pmod{q_0q}} - \frac{\mathbbm{1}_{(n, q_0q) = 1}}{\varphi(q_0q)} \omega_\eta(n; q_0q) \right) \right\vert, \\ \mathcal{S}_{\text{small}} &:= \sum_{\substack{q \sim Q \\ P^+(q) \le y_2 \\ (q, a_1a_2) = 1}} \frac{\tau_k(q)}{\varphi(q_0q)} \left\vert \sum_{\substack{n \le x \\ P^+(n) \le y_1}} \sum_{\substack{\chi \pmod{q_0 q} \\ 1 < \textnormal{cond}(\chi) \le x^\eta}} \chi(n) \right\vert. \end{aligned} \] For $\mathcal{S}_{\text{small}}$, we use the triangle inequality for the sum over $\chi$, and then proceed identically as in \cite[after (2.3)]{de2020niveau}; this gives the desired bound when $\delta$ is sufficiently small and $C$ is sufficiently large. For $\mathcal{S}_{\text{large}}$, we drop the smoothness condition on $q$, use the pointwise divisor bound $\tau_k(q) \ll_k q^{o(1)}$, group $q_0q$ into a new variable, and drop its divisibility constraint by $q_0$. Combined with \cref{eq:smooth-power-saving} (which followed from \cref{prop:triple-convo}), this gives \[ \mathcal{S}_{\text{large}} \ll_{\varepsilon,k} x^{1-\delta/3}, \] provided $\delta$ is sufficiently small and $C$ is sufficiently large in terms of $\varepsilon$. This is acceptable once $C$ is chosen to be large enough in terms of $\delta, A$, due to the bounds $x^{1-\delta/10} \ll_\delta \Psi(x, y_1) y_1^{-\delta/20}$, $Q^{1-\delta/10} \ll_\delta \Psi(Q, y_2)$, and $y_1 \ge (\log x)^C$, $q_0 \le x^{\delta/10}$.
nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 7.1
nodes.statement_short: Separate small-conductor characters; the small part follows de la Bretèche–Drappeau, the large part the power saving (6.10).

nodes.statement: For any $\varepsilon > 0$, there exist $C, \delta > 0$ such that the following holds. Let $x \ge 2$ and $a, b, c, d \in \mathbb{Z}$ satisfy $(a, c) = 1$, $ad - bc \neq 0$, and $|a|, |b|, |c|, |d| \le x^\delta$. Then for any $(\log x)^C \le y_1 \le y_2 \le x$ with $y_2 \le y_1^C$, one has \[ \#\{n \le x : P^+(an+b) \le y_1,\ P^+(cn+d) \le y_2\} \ll_\varepsilon \Psi(x, y_1) \varrho(u_2)^{5/8-\varepsilon}, \] where $u_2 := (\log x)/\log y_2$.
nodes.name: Smooth values of factorable quadratic polynomials
nodes.statement_short: Upper bound $\Psi(x,y_1)\varrho(u_2)^{5/8-\varepsilon}$ for $n$ with $an+b$ $y_1$-smooth and $cn+d$ $y_2$-smooth.

nodes.statement: This is identical to the proof of \cite[Th\'eor\`eme 4.1]{de2020niveau}, using \cref{thm:smooth-mod-smooth} instead of \cite[Th\'eor\`eme 2.1]{de2020niveau}. When applying \cref{thm:smooth-mod-smooth}, $q$ will be a divisor of $cn+d$ coming from an upper-bound sieve \cite[Proposition 3.1]{de2020niveau}, while $q_0 = a$, $a_1 = -(ad-bc)$, and $a_2 = c$; note that \[ q \mid cn+d \qquad\quad \iff \qquad\quad an+b \equiv a_1\overline{a_2} \pmod{q_0q}, \] and $P^+(an+b) \le y_1$, $P^+(q) \le y_2$.

nodes.statement: Take $(a, b, c, d) = (1, 0, 1, 1)$, $y_1 = y_2$ in \cref{cor:factorable-quadratic}, and use $\Psi(x, y_1) = x \varrho(u) e^{O(u)}$ where $u := (\log x)/\log y$ (see \cite[(1.7)]{de2020niveau} and \cite[(2.6) and (2.7)]{hildebrand1986number}).
